Annunciation. Leonardo's Annunciation, painted around 1472 to 1475 in Florence, depicts the moment when the angel Gabriel approaches the Virgin Mary to announce that she will bear the Christ Child. The work is executed in oil and tempera on poplar panel, measuring about 39 by 85 inches, and hangs now in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

Mary sits at a lectern, turning in surprise from her reading as the angel approaches from the left. Their spatial separation is spanned by interlocking gazes and gestures. Leonardo employs mathematical linear perspective with the receding wall and garden creating spatial depth, drawing the viewer's eye through the composition toward a distant landscape. The angel's extended arm and staff point toward Mary with deliberate geometry, while her hand expresses hesitation and receptive openness, a dialogue in gesture rather than words.

The garden setting contains flowering plants rendered with botanical precision, and roses that symbolize Mary's purity, grounding the sacred event in observed natural detail. Leonardo captures the moment before knowledge itself. Mary's expression combines wonder, uncertainty, and dawning comprehension, a psychological subtlety rare in earlier Annunciation paintings. The work shows influences from the Florentine tradition while announcing Leonardo's innovations: his soft modeling of light, his attention to narrative psychology, and his spatial mastery. It is an early work that established his distinctive approach to religious narrative.
